﴿So when the Inevitable Event occurs on that Day⟩ (al-Waqi'ah). Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: it is the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah).

The second: it is the Blast (al-Sayhah).

The third: it is the Hour in which creation will perish.

﴿And the heaven will be split open, for on that Day it will be frail⟩. Concerning its being split open there are two views:

The first: that its gates will be opened, related by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: that it will be split from the Milky Way (al-Majarrah), related by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

Concerning His words ﴿frail⟩ there are two views:

The first: torn apart (mutakharriqah), related by Ibn Shajarah. It is derived from their saying "wahā al-siqāʾ" (the waterskin became weak/torn) when it has ruptured, and from their proverbs:

"Leave the path of the one whose waterskin has gone slack, and whose water has been spilled in the desert,"

meaning: the one who is weak of intellect and does not protect himself.

The second: weak (daʿifah), related by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿And the angel will be upon its edges⟩. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: upon the edges of the heaven, and perhaps this is the statement of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: upon the edges of the world, related by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Concerning ﴿its edges⟩ (arjāʾihā) there are four views:

The first: upon its sides, related by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: upon its regions, related by al-Dahhak.

The third: its gates, related by al-Hasan.

The fourth: what is narrowest of it, related by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

The standing of the angels upon its edges is because of what they are commanded regarding the people of Paradise or Hellfire.

The second: eight rows of angels, related by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: that the bearers of the Throne are above the angels who are upon its edges.

The third: that they are above the people of the Resurrection.

(p-86) ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾. Muqatil said: The reason for this is that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said, "Muhammad is a sorcerer," Abu Jahl said, "He is a poet," and Uqba ibn Mu'ayt said, "He is a soothsayer." It may also carry a third meaning: "by what you know and what you do not know," as an emphasis on the all-inclusiveness of the oath.

The second: it is the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn Qutayba said: The Qur'an is not the speech of the Messenger; it is the speech of God and the conveying of the Messenger. So He suffices with the implication of the speech (fahwa al-kalam, the sense conveyed by the context) instead of mentioning it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 69, verse 44–52:

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings,﴾ meaning: if he had burdened himself to invent some lies against Us. He reports that the disbelievers of Quraysh said this about the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿We would have seized him by the right hand.﴾ Regarding this there are five interpretations:

First: We would have taken from him all of his strength. This is related from al-Rabi'.

Second: We would have seized him by the truth. This is related from al-Suddi and al-Hakam, and from it is the saying of the poet:

When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it with the right hand.

That is, by right (bi-al-istihqaq).

Third: We would have seized him by power. This is related from Mujahid.

Fourth: We would have cut off his right hand. This is related from al-Hasan.(p-87)

Fifth: Its meaning is that We would have taken him by his right hand in humiliation of him and contempt for him, as one says of what is meant as abasement: "Take him by his hand." This is related from Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

﴿Then We would have severed from him the aorta.﴾ Regarding this there are four sayings:

First: It is the nerve of the heart, called the cord of the heart, to which the heart is suspended. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: It is the heart together with its covering and what is adjacent to it. This is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Third: It is the cord that is in the back. This is related from Mujahid.

Fourth: It is a vein between the spinal cord (al-'ilba') and the windpipe (al-hulqum). This is related from al-Kalbi.

Regarding the indication of severing this, there are two views:

One: it is an expression of intent to kill him and destroy him, as the poet said:

When you reach me and bear my saddle, 'Arabah, then drink the blood of the aorta.

The second: what 'Ikrimah said, that the aorta, when it is cut, is neither a vein that is hungry nor a vein that is satisfied.

Second: steadfastness.

Third: admonition.

Fourth: salvation.
